decks.title: Nationalism in India — Part 1: War, Satyagraha and Non-Cooperation (1914–1922)
goals: Explain how the First World War changed life and politics in India
Explain the idea of satyagraha and Gandhiji's early movements
Describe the Rowlatt protests, Jallianwala Bagh, and the launch of the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements
Compare how towns, peasants, tribal groups and plantation workers understood swaraj
Answer a source-based question, a 5-mark question and a map question the way examiners mark them

slides.heading: Nationalism in India
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how a world war, a harsh law and a new method of protest turned Indian nationalism into a **mass movement** between 1914 and 1922.

nodes.label: 1914–18: First World War
1915: Gandhiji returns from South Africa
1917–18: Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad
1919: Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh
1921–22: Non-Cooperation and Khilafat

visual.alt: Timeline of Part 1: the First World War from 1914 to 1918, Gandhiji's return in 1915, the satyagrahas of 1917 and 1918, the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh in 1919, and the Non-Cooperation and Khilafat movements of 1921 and 1922
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! In the last chapter we saw how nations were made in Europe. In India, the story is tied to the fight against colonial rule. People who had very different lives, a mill worker in Ahmedabad, a tenant in Awadh, a student in Lahore, discovered that they shared one opponent. In Part 1 we follow how that discovery happened between 1914 and 1922. Keep an eye on the dates on this timeline.

slides.heading: One struggle, many grievances
slides.body_md: Anti-colonial nationalism grew as people felt the **weight of colonial rule** in their own lives. Different groups joined for **different reasons**, and the Congress tried to hold them together.

headers: What hurt them under colonial rule
rows: High rents and revenue, forced labour
Closure of forests they depended on
Low wages, harsh rules on movement

visual.alt: Table: the urban middle class resented insult and lack of rights; peasants faced high rents and forced labour; tribal communities lost access to forests; workers suffered low wages and restrictions on movement

slides.narration: Here is the key idea of the whole chapter. Nationalism in India was not one feeling shared in the same way by everyone. A lawyer, a peasant, a forest dweller and a tea-garden worker each felt colonial rule pressing on them in a different place. The challenge for the Congress was to bring these different hopes under one banner. Watch for this tension in every movement we study.

slides.heading: The First World War and India
slides.body_md: The war of 1914–18 changed both the **economy** and the **politics** of India.

rows: Defence spending financed by war loans, higher customs duties and a new income tax
Soldiers raised by forced recruitment in villages
Crop failures (1918–19, 1920–21) and an influenza epidemic

visual.alt: Table of the burdens of the First World War: defence spending financed through loans and taxes including a new income tax; prices doubling between 1913 and 1918; forced recruitment; crop failures and an influenza epidemic that caused food shortages and millions of deaths

slides.narration: War is expensive, and India paid for Britain's war. Defence spending rose, so the government borrowed, raised customs duties and introduced income tax. Prices roughly doubled between 1913 and 1918. In villages, young men were pushed into the army. Then harvests failed and an influenza epidemic swept the country. People expected their hardships to end after the war. When they did not, the anger had to go somewhere.

slides.heading: Gandhiji and the idea of satyagraha
slides.body_md: Gandhiji returned to India in **January 1915** after fighting racist laws in South Africa with a new method he called **satyagraha**.

nodes.label: Stand firmly for truth
Refuse to use violence
Accept suffering patiently
Appeal to the opponent's conscience
Opponent is persuaded to change

visual.alt: Flow: standing for truth, refusing violence and accepting suffering lead to an appeal to the opponent's conscience, which persuades the opponent to change
visual.caption: How a satyagrahi hopes to win

slides.narration: Satyagraha joins two words: truth and firmness. Gandhiji argued that if your cause is just, you do not need to hurt your opponent. Instead, you stand firm, refuse violence and accept punishment calmly. Your patience exposes the injustice and appeals to the conscience of the other side. He had used this method in South Africa, and he believed it could unite all Indians, because anyone could take part.

slides.heading: Testing satyagraha: 1917–1918

rows: Crop failure and plague; could not pay revenue, asked for relief

visual.alt: Table of Gandhiji's early satyagrahas: Champaran in Bihar in 1917 against the indigo plantation system; Kheda in Gujarat in 1917 and 1918 for peasants who could not pay revenue after crop failure and plague; Ahmedabad in 1918 for cotton mill workers
visual.caption: Learn these three for map work too

slides.narration: Before any national campaign, Gandhiji tried his method locally. In Champaran in Bihar he stood with peasants against the indigo planters. In Kheda in Gujarat, peasants hit by crop failure and plague could not pay revenue, and he supported their demand for relief. In Ahmedabad he took up the cause of cotton mill workers. Learn these three as a set: they come up in map questions every year.

slides.heading: Quick check: early movements
slides.body_md: Put these events in order.
slides.narration: Try ordering these four events. Start by writing the year next to each one.

slides.heading: The Rowlatt Act and the hartal of 1919
slides.body_md: In 1919 the **Rowlatt Act** was rushed through the Imperial Legislative Council in spite of the **united opposition of its Indian members**. It allowed detention **without trial for two years**.

nodes.label: Rowlatt Act passed
6 April: nationwide hartal
Local leaders arrested
10 April: police fire on a procession in Amritsar
Martial law; General Dyer in command

visual.alt: Flow: the Rowlatt Act led to a nationwide hartal on 6 April 1919, arrests of local leaders, police firing on a procession in Amritsar on 10 April and martial law under General Dyer

slides.narration: The Rowlatt Act gave the government sweeping powers to crush political activity and to hold people without trial for two years. Every Indian member of the council opposed it, but it was passed anyway. Gandhiji called for a non-violent protest beginning with a hartal on the sixth of April, nineteen nineteen. Shops closed and rallies were held. The government answered with arrests, and in Amritsar the police fired on a procession.

slides.heading: 13 April 1919: Jallianwala Bagh
slides.body_md: On **Baisakhi**, a large crowd gathered in the enclosed ground of **Jallianwala Bagh** in Amritsar. Many were villagers attending the fair who did not know of martial law. **General Dyer** blocked the exits and ordered his troops to fire. **Hundreds** were killed.

rows: Crowds came out in many north Indian towns
Strikes, clashes with police, attacks on government buildings
Indians lost faith in British justice

visual.alt: Table: Dyer wanted to terrorise people and restore order, but crowds came out across north Indian towns, there were strikes and clashes, and Indians lost faith in British justice

slides.narration: This is one of the darkest days in our history. The crowd at Jallianwala Bagh was peaceful, and many had simply come for the Baisakhi fair. Dyer later admitted that his aim was to terrify people into obeying. The result was the reverse. Protests broke out across north India, and the government responded with brutal repression. Seeing the violence grow, Gandhiji called the satyagraha off.

slides.heading: The Khilafat issue: a bridge between communities

nodes.label: Ottoman Turkey defeated in the war
Rumours of a harsh treaty for the Sultan (Khalifa)
Khilafat Committee, Bombay, March 1919 (Muhammad Ali, Shaukat Ali)
Gandhiji sees a chance for Hindu–Muslim unity
Calcutta, Sept 1920: leaders agree to non-cooperation for Khilafat and swaraj

visual.alt: Flow: Ottoman defeat leads to rumours of a harsh treaty for the Khalifa, the formation of the Khilafat Committee in Bombay in March 1919 under the Ali brothers, Gandhiji's decision to seek Hindu–Muslim unity, and the Calcutta session of September 1920 agreeing to non-cooperation

slides.narration: The Khalifa was the Ottoman Sultan, seen by many Muslims as their spiritual head. After the war there were rumours that the victors would impose a harsh treaty on him. In March nineteen nineteen the Ali brothers formed the Khilafat Committee in Bombay. Gandhiji saw an opportunity: a movement in which Hindus and Muslims fought side by side would be far stronger. At the Calcutta session of September nineteen twenty, he persuaded other leaders to agree.

slides.heading: Why non-cooperation? The idea and the plan
slides.body_md: In ***Hind Swaraj*** (1909) Gandhiji argued that British rule **depended on Indian cooperation**. Withdraw it, and the rule would collapse.

nodes.label: Stage 1: give up government titles
Stage 2: boycott civil services, army, police, courts, councils, schools and foreign goods
Stage 3: full civil disobedience if the government turns to repression

visual.alt: Flow of the planned stages of non-cooperation: first giving up titles, then boycotting services, courts, councils, schools and foreign goods, and finally full civil disobedience if the government used repression
visual.caption: Adopted at the Nagpur session, December 1920; launched January 1921

slides.narration: Here is Gandhiji's argument in one line. The British ruled India with Indian help: Indian clerks, soldiers, police and lawyers. If Indians stopped helping, the system would stop working. The plan was to move in stages. First, return titles. Then boycott government jobs, courts, councils, schools and foreign cloth. Only if the government cracked down would people go further and break laws. The plan was adopted at Nagpur in December nineteen twenty.

slides.heading: Quick check: the Rowlatt Act
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true, and whether the reason explains the assertion.
slides.narration: Judge each statement on its own first, then ask whether the reason really explains the assertion.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a source-based question, step by step
slides.body_md: Source (written by SOYL): *An imagined letter from a law student in Lahore, February 1921, says he has left his government college, his father has stopped attending court, and the family burnt their foreign shirts in the square; but his friend has gone back to college because the new national college has only two teachers.*
bullets: Step 1 — Read the questions first, then the source.
Step 2 — (a) "Name the movement" (1 mark): one precise answer, the Non-Cooperation Movement.
Step 3 — (b) "State one form of protest in the letter" (1 mark): lift it from the source, e.g. leaving a government college.
Step 4 — (c) "Why did the friend go back?" (2 marks): one point from the source (too few teachers) plus one from your knowledge (alternative institutions came up slowly; khadi was costly).
Step 5 — Keep (c) to about 40 words.

rows: Any one protest named in the source
1 for the source point + 1 for linking to wider knowledge

visual.alt: Table: part a earns one mark for naming the movement; part b one mark for a protest from the source; part c two marks, one from the source and one from wider knowledge

slides.narration: Source questions reward a method. Read the questions first so you know what to hunt for. One-mark parts want one precise fact, often sitting in the source. The two-mark part is where marks slip away. Examiners want one point from the source and one point from your own knowledge. Here, the source tells us the new college had too few teachers, and you add that such institutions came up slowly.

slides.heading: Non-cooperation in the towns

rows: Boycotted council elections in most provinces (not in Madras, where the non-Brahman Justice Party contested)
Boycotted foreign cloth, burnt it in bonfires, picketed liquor shops

visual.alt: Table of urban participation: students left schools, teachers resigned, lawyers gave up practice, council elections were boycotted except in Madras where the Justice Party contested, and traders and crowds boycotted foreign cloth and picketed liquor shops

slides.narration: City dwellers of the middle class were the first to respond. Students by the thousand quit government schools and colleges, teachers handed in resignations, and lawyers stopped appearing in court. Council elections were boycotted almost everywhere. Madras was the exception: the Justice Party, a party of non-Brahmans, saw the council as its chance to gain power. Foreign cloth was burnt in huge bonfires, imports of foreign cloth fell sharply, and Indian mills and handlooms sold more.

slides.heading: Why the movement slowed in the cities
columns:
**Problem 1: the price of khadi**

- Hand-spun, hand-woven khadi usually cost more than mill cloth.
- Poorer people could not keep buying it.

**Problem 2: no alternatives**

- National schools, colleges and courts were slow to come up.
- Students and teachers went back to government schools; lawyers returned to court.

nodes.label: Boycott of foreign cloth and institutions
Khadi costly; few Indian alternatives
Many people drift back
Movement slows in towns

visual.alt: Flow: the boycott ran into the high cost of khadi and the shortage of Indian alternatives, so many people drifted back and the movement slowed in the towns

slides.narration: A boycott only works if people have something to use instead. Khadi was made by hand, so it usually cost more than mill cloth, and poor families simply could not afford to keep buying it. In the same way, you cannot boycott a government college for long if there is no other college to go to. So many students, teachers and lawyers went back. The movement in the towns slowly lost force.

slides.heading: Peasants of Awadh
slides.body_md: In Awadh, peasants led by **Baba Ramchandra**, a sanyasi who had been an indentured labourer in **Fiji**, rose against **talukdars and landlords**.

rows: Very high rents and many cesses
Nai-dhobi bandhs: landlords denied barbers and washermen
Led by Jawaharlal Nehru, Baba Ramchandra and others
In 1921 some attacks on talukdars' houses and grain hoards

visual.alt: Table: Awadh peasants faced high rents, begar and eviction; they used nai-dhobi bandhs, refused begar and in 1921 some attacked talukdars' houses; the Oudh Kisan Sabha formed in October 1920 under Nehru, Baba Ramchandra and others had over 300 branches within a month

slides.narration: In the countryside, swaraj took on a very local meaning. In Awadh, tenants paid crushing rents and were forced to work for landlords for nothing. That unpaid work is called begar. Baba Ramchandra, who had once laboured in Fiji, organised them. Panchayats ordered that no barber or washerman should serve an oppressive landlord. In nineteen twenty-one some protests turned violent, and local leaders wrongly claimed Gandhiji had approved.

slides.heading: Tribal peasants of the Gudem Hills
slides.body_md: In the **Gudem Hills** of Andhra Pradesh, a guerrilla movement grew in the early 1920s under **Alluri Sitarama Raju**.

nodes.label: Large forest areas closed: no grazing, fuelwood or fruit
Begar for road building
Raju: inspired by non-cooperation but believes in force
Attacks on police stations
Raju captured and executed, 1924

visual.alt: Flow: closure of forests and begar for road building led people to follow Raju, who was inspired by non-cooperation but believed in force; his followers attacked police stations, and he was captured and executed in 1924

slides.narration: For forest communities, the colonial forest laws were the problem. Forests they had always used were shut to them: no grazing, no firewood, no wild fruit, and they were forced to build roads without pay. Alluri Sitarama Raju admired Gandhiji and asked people to give up drinking, yet he believed that only force could free India. His followers fought a guerrilla war. He was captured and executed in nineteen twenty-four, and became a folk hero.

slides.heading: Plantation workers of Assam
slides.body_md: Under the **Inland Emigration Act of 1859**, tea-garden workers could not leave without permission.

nodes.label: Hear of non-cooperation
Thousands leave the plantations for home
Stranded by a railway and steamer strike
Caught and beaten by police

visual.alt: Flow: Assam plantation workers heard of non-cooperation, thousands left for home, were stranded by a railway and steamer strike, and were caught and beaten by the police

slides.narration: For tea-garden workers in Assam, freedom had a very concrete meaning: being able to walk out of the gates. A law of eighteen fifty-nine tied them to the gardens. When news of the movement reached them, thousands left and set off for their villages, believing a new order had arrived. They were stranded when railway and steamer workers went on strike, and the police caught them and beat them badly.

slides.heading: One word, many meanings of swaraj

rows: Boycott of British institutions and goods; self-rule
End of high rents and begar
Return of forest rights; end of forced labour
Freedom to leave the gardens and go home

visual.alt: Table: for the urban middle class swaraj meant boycott and self-rule; for Awadh peasants an end to high rents and begar; for tribal people forest rights; for Assam plantation workers freedom to go home

slides.narration: Here is the big picture for this topic. Every group heard the same word, swaraj, and filled it with its own hopes. For a lawyer it meant self-rule. For a tenant it meant lower rent. For a forest dweller it meant forests open again, and for a tea worker it meant going home. Examiners love asking you to compare these. A tidy table like this one is the best way to revise.

slides.heading: Quick check: the movement begins
slides.body_md: True or false?
slides.narration: Decide whether the statement is true. Remember which session adopted the programme and when the movement actually began.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a 5-mark answer that scores full marks
slides.body_md: Question: *"The Non-Cooperation Movement meant different things to different people." Explain with five points.* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — Open with one line: each group joined for its own grievances.
Step 2 — Plan five distinct groups: town middle class, Awadh peasants, Gudem tribal people, Assam workers, and Muslims of the Khilafat movement.
Step 3 — For each: who, what they did, what swaraj meant, with a key term (begar, nai-dhobi bandh, Inland Emigration Act).
Step 4 — Do not write two points about the same group.
Step 5 — Close with a one-line judgement if words remain.

headers: Key term the examiner looks for
rows: Students, lawyers; boycott of schools, courts, cloth

visual.alt: Table of five points for the model answer, one mark each: town middle class and boycott; Baba Ramchandra and begar; Raju and forest closure; the Inland Emigration Act; Khilafat and Hindu Muslim unity

slides.narration: A five-mark answer is five separate ideas, each worth a mark. Plan first. Here the plan is simple: five different groups. For each one, say who they were, what they did, and what swaraj meant to them, and drop in a key term the examiner is scanning for. The commonest mistake is writing three points about the towns and only one about the villages. Spread your points.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: map work
slides.body_md: Task: *On an outline map of India, locate and label (A) the district of the 1917 indigo satyagraha, (B) the city of the 1918 mill workers' satyagraha, and (C) the site of the firing of 13 April 1919.*
bullets: Step 1 — Decode the clues: indigo 1917 → Champaran; mill workers 1918 → Ahmedabad; 13 April 1919 → Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar.
Step 2 — Find a landmark: Champaran is in north-west Bihar on the Nepal border.
Step 3 — Ahmedabad is in Gujarat on the Sabarmati; Kheda lies just south of it.
Step 4 — Amritsar is in Punjab near the border with Pakistan.
Step 5 — Mark each with a dot, write the name beside it, and label clearly.

visual.alt: Table of clues and places: indigo 1917 is Champaran in north-west Bihar; mill workers 1918 is Ahmedabad in Gujarat; the firing of 13 April 1919 is Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, Punjab

slides.narration: Map questions are easy marks if you prepare. First turn each clue into a name. Then use a landmark to find it: a border, a river or a coast. Champaran sits in the north-west corner of Bihar, touching Nepal. Ahmedabad stands on the Sabarmati in Gujarat, with Kheda just to its south. Amritsar is in Punjab, close to the border. A dot and a neat label earn the mark.

slides.heading: 1922: the movement is called off
slides.body_md: In **February 1922**, a peaceful demonstration at **Chauri Chaura** (Gorakhpur) turned into a violent clash with the police. Gandhiji **withdrew** the movement.

rows: Contest elections to the councils set up by the Act of 1919 and oppose policies from inside
More radical mass agitation and full independence
Training satyagrahis before another mass struggle

visual.alt: Table: after 1922 the Swaraj Party of C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru wanted to enter the councils; younger leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose wanted radical agitation and full independence; Gandhiji wanted satyagrahis trained first

slides.narration: By early nineteen twenty-two the movement was turning violent in places. After the clash at Chauri Chaura, Gandhiji called it off. He believed people first had to learn the discipline of non-violence before any new mass campaign. The Congress then divided. Some leaders formed the Swaraj Party to fight elections and work inside the councils. Younger leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pushed for bolder action and complete independence.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Taxes, doubled prices, forced recruitment, famine and epidemic
Truth and non-violence; Champaran 1917, Kheda 1917–18, Ahmedabad 1918
Rowlatt Act, hartal 6 April, Jallianwala Bagh 13 April
Ali brothers; Calcutta Sept 1920, Nagpur Dec 1920; launched Jan 1921
Towns, Awadh, Gudem Hills, Assam: different meanings of swaraj

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: war burdens; satyagraha and the three early movements; the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh in 1919; Khilafat and the Non-Cooperation sessions of 1920; the different strands; and the withdrawal in 1922

slides.narration: Let us pull Part 1 together. The war left Indians poorer and angrier. Gandhiji offered a new method, satyagraha, and tested it in Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad. The Rowlatt Act and the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh turned anger into protest. The Khilafat issue brought Hindus and Muslims together, and non-cooperation began in January nineteen twenty-one. Each group read swaraj in its own way, until Chauri Chaura led to withdrawal.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Know the dates: 1915, 1917, 1918, 6 and 13 April 1919, Sept and Dec 1920, Jan 1921, Feb 1922.
Calcutta (Sept 1920) agreed to the plan; Nagpur (Dec 1920) adopted the programme. Do not swap them.
Kheda = revenue relief after crop failure and plague; Champaran = indigo. Easy to mix up.
Madras was the exception to the council boycott (Justice Party).
For "different meanings of swaraj", give one group per point with a key term.
Map work: Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad, Amritsar, Calcutta, Nagpur — dot and label.
slides.narration: Before your test, check these traps. Students often swap the Calcutta and Nagpur sessions: Calcutta agreed, Nagpur adopted. Another favourite mix-up is Champaran and Kheda. Remember, indigo means Champaran. If you are asked how different groups understood swaraj, write one group per point, each with its own key term. And practise your map: these places appear in the board paper every year.

decks.title: Nationalism in India — Part 2: Civil Disobedience and the Sense of Belonging (1928–1934)
goals: Explain the Simon Commission, the Lahore Congress and the Salt March
Compare the participation of rich and poor peasants, business classes, workers and women in Civil Disobedience
Explain the limits of the movement for Dalits and Muslims
Analyse how history, folklore, songs, images and symbols created a sense of nationhood
Locate Congress session cities and satyagraha sites on a map of India

slides.heading: Nationalism in India: towards Civil Disobedience
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how a march to the sea in **1930** drew millions into breaking colonial laws, who joined, who held back, and how Indians came to **imagine one nation**.

nodes.label: 1928: Simon Commission
Dec 1929: Lahore Congress, Purna Swaraj
1930: Salt March
1931: Gandhi–Irwin Pact
1932: Poona Pact
1934: movement loses momentum

visual.alt: Timeline of Part 2: the Simon Commission in 1928, the Lahore Congress and Purna Swaraj in December 1929, the Salt March in 1930, the Gandhi Irwin Pact in 1931, the Poona Pact in 1932 and the loss of momentum by 1934
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 2. After nineteen twenty-two, the national movement seemed to lose its way. Then, within a few years, it rose again, bigger than before. This time people were asked not just to stop cooperating, but to break laws. We will see why salt became the symbol, who joined and who stayed away, and how songs, pictures and flags made people feel they belonged to one nation.

slides.heading: The late 1920s: depression and a commission

rows: Agricultural prices fell from 1926 and collapsed after 1930
Peasants could not sell harvests or pay revenue
All-British body to review India's constitution; no Indian member
Congress and Muslim League both protest
Vague promise of dominion status and a Round Table Conference

visual.alt: Table: falling agricultural prices from 1926 and a collapse after 1930 hurt peasants; the all-British Simon Commission arrived in 1928 and met protests from the Congress and the Muslim League; in October 1929 Irwin offered vague dominion status and a Round Table Conference

slides.narration: Two forces revived the movement. First, a worldwide economic depression. Farm prices began falling in nineteen twenty-six and collapsed after nineteen thirty, so peasants could not sell their crops or pay revenue. Second, a political insult. Britain sent the Simon Commission to review India's constitution, and not one member was Indian. Everywhere it went, it was met with black flags and the slogan, go back Simon.

slides.heading: From Irwin's offer to Purna Swaraj

nodes.label: Irwin offers dominion status "in an unspecified future"
Radicals (Nehru, Bose) want full independence
Lahore Congress, Dec 1929, under Jawaharlal Nehru: Purna Swaraj
26 January 1930: Independence Day pledge

visual.alt: Flow: Irwin's vague offer of dominion status did not satisfy radicals like Nehru and Bose; the Lahore Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru in December 1929 adopted Purna Swaraj; 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day

slides.narration: The Viceroy, Lord Irwin, tried to calm things with a vague promise of dominion status at some unnamed future date, and a round table conference. It did not satisfy the younger leaders. In December nineteen twenty-nine, at Lahore, the Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru declared that its goal was Purna Swaraj, complete independence. On the twenty-sixth of January nineteen thirty, people took a pledge for independence. But the date drew only limited attention at first.

slides.heading: Quick check: Lahore 1929
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank.
slides.narration: One word, or two, is all you need here. Think of what the Lahore session made its goal.

slides.heading: The Salt March, step by step

rows: Gandhiji writes to Viceroy Irwin with eleven demands; the most stirring is to abolish the salt tax
March begins from Sabarmati ashram with 78 volunteers
About 240 miles in 24 days, roughly 10 miles a day; crowds gather in every village
At Dandi, Gandhiji makes salt by boiling sea water, breaking the law

visual.alt: Table of the Salt March: on 31 January 1930 Gandhiji sent eleven demands to Irwin, the deadline of 11 March passed, the march began from Sabarmati with 78 volunteers on 12 March, covered about 240 miles in 24 days, and on 6 April at Dandi Gandhiji made salt from sea water

slides.narration: Gandhiji first wrote to the Viceroy with eleven demands, some for industrialists, some for peasants, and one for everyone: abolish the salt tax. If they were not met by the eleventh of March, he would begin civil disobedience. They were not. So on the twelfth of March he set out from Sabarmati with seventy-eight volunteers. Twenty-four days and about two hundred and forty miles later, at Dandi, he broke the salt law.

slides.heading: Why salt?

nodes.label: Every household, rich or poor, needs salt
Salt is taxed, and only the government may make it
The tax shows the oppressive face of British rule
Anyone near the coast can break the law by making salt
A symbol that can unite the whole country

visual.alt: Flow: because every household needs salt and the government taxes it and controls its manufacture, the tax shows the oppressive side of British rule; because anyone can make salt, breaking the law is easy; together salt becomes a uniting symbol

slides.narration: Why choose something as ordinary as salt? Precisely because it is ordinary. The richest family and the poorest labourer both put salt in their food, and both paid the tax. Only the government was allowed to make it. So the tax showed British rule at its most unfair, and breaking the law was something anyone could do. A simple pinch of salt became a symbol the whole country could understand.

slides.heading: How Civil Disobedience spread
slides.body_md: This time people were called on to **break colonial laws openly**, going beyond **refusing cooperation**.

rows: Making salt; demonstrating at government salt factories
Thousands in many parts of the country
Boycott of foreign cloth; picketing of liquor shops
Entering reserved forests to collect wood and graze cattle

visual.alt: Table of forms of civil disobedience: making salt, boycotting foreign cloth and picketing liquor shops, refusing revenue and chaukidari taxes, resignations of village officials, and violation of forest laws by forest communities

slides.narration: Civil disobedience went further than non-cooperation. Non-cooperation meant stepping back from the government. Civil disobedience meant openly breaking its laws. Thousands made salt and protested at salt factories. Foreign cloth was boycotted and liquor shops picketed. Peasants refused to pay revenue and chaukidari taxes, village officials resigned, and forest people walked into reserved forests to collect wood and graze cattle.

slides.heading: Repression, a pact, and a second round

nodes.label: April 1930: Abdul Ghaffar Khan arrested; firing on crowds in Peshawar
May 1930: Gandhiji arrested; workers in Sholapur attack government buildings
5 March 1931: Gandhi–Irwin Pact
Dec 1931: Second Round Table Conference fails
1932: movement relaunched; by 1934 it loses momentum

visual.alt: Flow: Ghaffar Khan's arrest in April 1930 and firing in Peshawar; Gandhiji's arrest in May 1930 and attacks by Sholapur workers; the Gandhi Irwin Pact on 5 March 1931; the failure of the Second Round Table Conference in December 1931; relaunch in 1932 and loss of momentum by 1934

slides.narration: The government struck back. In April nineteen thirty Abdul Ghaffar Khan was arrested and troops fired on crowds in Peshawar. A month later Gandhiji himself was arrested, and mill workers in Sholapur attacked police posts and government buildings. Alarmed, Gandhiji called off the movement and signed a pact with Irwin in March nineteen thirty-one. Talks in London failed, the movement restarted, and by nineteen thirty-four it had faded.

slides.heading: Peasants: rich and poor
columns:
**Rich peasants** (Patidars of Gujarat, Jats of UP)

- Grew commercial crops; hit by falling prices
- Wanted revenue reduced; refused to pay
- Disappointed when the movement ended in 1931 with no revenue cut; many stayed away in 1932

**Poor peasants** (often tenants)

- Could not pay rent on rented land
- Wanted unpaid rent remitted
- Joined radical movements, often led by Socialists and Communists
- Congress hesitated to back "no rent" campaigns

slides.narration: Peasants were not one group. Rich peasant communities, such as the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh, grew crops for the market. When prices crashed, they could not pay revenue, so they backed the movement keenly. Poor peasants usually rented land. They wanted their rent cancelled, which meant taking on rich peasants and landlords. The Congress feared upsetting those landlords, so poor peasants often turned to more radical leaders.

rows: Protection against foreign imports; a rupee–sterling rate that discouraged imports
Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress (1920); FICCI (1927)
Freedom from colonial controls on business
Fear of long disruption after the Round Table Conference failed
They gave money and refused to buy or sell imported goods
Rising influence of socialism among young Congress members

visual.alt: Table: business classes joined for protection against imports and freedom from colonial controls through bodies like FICCI with leaders like Thakurdas and Birla, giving money and refusing imports; they drew back because of militant activity, fear of disruption after the Round Table Conference and rising socialism

slides.narration: Indian industrialists had made big profits during the war and wanted to grow further. They resented colonial policies that favoured imports. Through bodies like the Federation of Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries, formed in nineteen twenty-seven, leaders such as Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G D Birla backed the movement with money and boycotts. But after the London talks failed, they worried about disorder, long disruption and the socialist ideas of younger Congress members.

Mostly from high-caste urban and rich peasant families; no posts of authority in the Congress

slides.narration: Industrial workers joined in large numbers only around Nagpur. Some went on strike, and tin miners in Chotanagpur wore Gandhi caps at rallies. But the Congress kept workers' demands at arm's length, fearing it would lose the industrialists. Women, on the other hand, came out in very large numbers. They marched, made salt and picketed shops. Yet the Congress was slow to give them any real authority inside the organisation.

slides.narration: Many Dalits were wary of a Congress that did not want to upset orthodox Hindus. Gandhiji fought untouchability through temple entry, wells and schools, but many Dalit leaders sought political answers. Doctor Ambedkar demanded separate electorates. When the British agreed, Gandhiji fasted, believing this would divide society. The Poona Pact settled it: reserved seats, but elected by all voters. Both men cared about the same people; they disagreed about the remedy.

slides.heading: The limits of the movement: Muslims

Jayakar of the Hindu Mahasabha opposed compromise and hopes faded

slides.narration: Large sections of Muslims also kept their distance in nineteen thirty. After the Khilafat years, the Congress came to be linked in many minds with Hindu religious groups, and communal riots deepened suspicion. Muhammad Ali Jinnah was ready to give up separate electorates if Muslims were assured fair representation. But at the All Parties Conference of nineteen twenty-eight, M R Jayakar of the Hindu Mahasabha strongly opposed compromise, and the chance was lost.

slides.body_md: A nation is felt when people **imagine** themselves as one community. Images gave India a **face**.

slides.narration: How do millions of strangers come to feel they belong to one nation? Partly through pictures and songs. In the eighteen seventies Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote Vande Mataram, a hymn to the motherland. Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata as a calm, spiritual woman. Over time she was shown in many forms, and devotion to this mother figure came to stand for love of the nation.

Recovered a culture seen as truly national

slides.narration: Nationalists also turned to folk tales and songs, believing they held the real culture of the people. Rabindranath Tagore collected ballads and rhymes, and Natesa Sastri gathered Tamil folk tales. Flags became powerful too. The Swadeshi flag of Bengal had eight lotuses and a crescent. Gandhiji's Swaraj flag carried a spinning wheel. And writers retold India's ancient achievements to answer British claims that Indians were backward.

slides.heading: A sense of belonging, and its blind spots
slides.body_md: Symbols drawn from **one tradition** could unite many people, but also make others feel left out.

slides.narration: Every symbol speaks more clearly to some people than to others. Histories that praised a Hindu golden age, and images drawn from Hindu worship, inspired many. But people of other communities could feel that this nation was not quite theirs. That is a useful point for evaluation questions: the tools that built national feeling also had limits. A balanced answer mentions both the unity and the exclusion.

sections.heading: 1. The war, satyagraha and the first experiments

key_terms.definition_md: A method of mass protest based on truth and non-violence that seeks to persuade the opponent rather than defeat him by force.
Compelling villagers to join the army, common during the First World War.

sections.heading: 2. Rowlatt, Jallianwala Bagh, Khilafat and the plan of non-cooperation
sections.body_md:
**Rowlatt Act (1919).** Passed in spite of the **united opposition of the Indian members** of the Imperial Legislative Council, it gave the government sweeping powers to repress political activity and allowed detention **without trial for two years**. Gandhiji called a nationwide satyagraha beginning with a **hartal on 6 April 1919**.

In Amritsar, local leaders were arrested and police fired on a procession on **10 April**; **martial law** followed under **General Dyer**. On **13 April 1919** (Baisakhi) Dyer blocked the exits of **Jallianwala Bagh** and fired on a crowd, many of them villagers at the fair who did not know of martial law. Hundreds died. Protests, strikes and clashes spread in north India; as violence grew, Gandhiji called off the Rowlatt satyagraha.

**Khilafat.** After the Ottoman defeat there were rumours of a harsh treaty for the Sultan, the **Khalifa**. A **Khilafat Committee** was formed in **Bombay in March 1919** under **Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali**. Gandhiji saw a chance for **Hindu–Muslim unity**.

**The plan.** In ***Hind Swaraj*** (1909) Gandhiji argued that the British could rule India only as long as Indians worked with them. At the **Calcutta session (September 1920)** he persuaded other leaders to start non-cooperation for Khilafat and swaraj; at **Nagpur (December 1920)** a compromise was reached and the programme adopted. The stages: give up **titles** → boycott **civil services, army, police, courts, councils, schools and foreign goods** → full **civil disobedience** if the government turned to repression. The movement began in **January 1921**.

key_terms.definition_md: A 1919 law allowing detention of political prisoners without trial for two years.
A protest in which shops, offices and work are shut down.
The movement to defend the position of the Ottoman Sultan as Khalifa, spiritual head of many Muslims.
Rule by military authorities in place of ordinary civil law.

sections.heading: 3. Differing strands within the movement
sections.body_md:
**Towns.** Students quit government schools and colleges, teachers and headmasters resigned, and lawyers stopped appearing in court. Council elections were boycotted in most provinces except **Madras**, where the **Justice Party** of non-Brahmans contested them as a route to power. Foreign cloth was burnt, liquor shops picketed, cloth imports fell sharply and Indian mills and handlooms gained. The movement slowed because **khadi was costlier** than mill cloth and **Indian institutions came up slowly**.

**Awadh.** **Baba Ramchandra**, a sanyasi who had been an **indentured labourer in Fiji**, led peasants against **talukdars and landlords** who demanded very high rents, cesses and **begar**. Demands: lower rent, end of begar, social boycott of oppressive landlords through **nai-dhobi bandhs**. Jawaharlal Nehru toured Awadh villages in June 1920; the **Oudh Kisan Sabha** was set up by **October 1920** and had over 300 branches within a month. In **1921** some actions turned violent; local leaders falsely claimed Gandhiji had approved no-tax and land seizure.

**Gudem Hills (Andhra Pradesh).** Colonial forest closure denied people grazing, fuelwood and fruit, and they resented **begar** for roads. **Alluri Sitarama Raju**, inspired by non-cooperation but convinced that force was needed, led a **guerrilla** movement; his followers attacked police stations. He was captured and executed in **1924**.

**Assam plantations.** The **Inland Emigration Act of 1859** stopped workers from leaving without permission. In 1921 thousands walked out and set off for their villages; stranded by a railway and steamer strike, they were caught and beaten by police.

**Withdrawal.** After a violent clash at **Chauri Chaura** (Gorakhpur) in **February 1922**, Gandhiji called off the movement. **C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru** formed the **Swaraj Party** to contest council elections; **Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose** wanted more radical action and full independence.

key_terms.definition_md: Forced labour without payment.
A social boycott in which barbers and washermen refused to serve an oppressive landlord.
A large landholder in Awadh who collected rent from tenants.
A worker bound by contract to work for an employer for a fixed period, often overseas.

rows: Forest rights; end of forced labour
Freedom to leave and go home

sections.heading: 4. Towards Civil Disobedience
sections.body_md:
**Background.** Agricultural prices began to fall from **1926** and collapsed after **1930** in the world depression. The **Simon Commission**, set up by the Tory government, arrived in **1928** to review India's constitution; it had **no Indian member** and was met with "Go back Simon" protests by the Congress and the Muslim League. In **October 1929** Lord Irwin offered **dominion status** in an unspecified future and a **Round Table Conference**.

**Lahore, December 1929.** Under **Jawaharlal Nehru** the Congress formalised the demand for **Purna Swaraj**; **26 January 1930** was observed as Independence Day.

**The Salt March.** On **31 January 1930** Gandhiji sent Irwin **eleven demands**, the most important being the abolition of the **salt tax**, with a deadline of **11 March**. On **12 March** he set out from **Sabarmati** with **78 volunteers**, walking about **240 miles in 24 days**. On **6 April** at **Dandi** he made salt by boiling sea water. Salt worked as a symbol because it was used by rich and poor alike and its manufacture was a **government monopoly**.

**Civil disobedience** asked people to **break colonial laws**, not only to refuse cooperation: salt was made, foreign cloth boycotted, liquor shops picketed, **revenue and chaukidari taxes** refused, village officials resigned and forest laws broken.

**Repression and truce.** **Abdul Ghaffar Khan** was arrested in **April 1930** and troops fired on crowds in Peshawar; Gandhiji was arrested a month later, and workers in **Sholapur** attacked government buildings. The **Gandhi–Irwin Pact (5 March 1931)**: Gandhiji agreed to attend the Round Table Conference (the Congress had boycotted the first) and the government agreed to release political prisoners. The Second Round Table Conference in London (December 1931) failed. The movement was relaunched in 1932 and had lost momentum by **1934**.

key_terms.definition_md: Complete independence, the goal adopted at the Lahore Congress of 1929.
Deliberately breaking unjust laws without violence, as a form of protest.
Self-government within the British Empire, with Britain's monarch as head of state.

visual.alt: Timeline table: Simon Commission 1928, Lahore Congress December 1929, Salt March March to April 1930, Gandhi Irwin Pact March 1931, Second Round Table Conference December 1931, loss of momentum by 1934

sections.heading: 5. Who joined Civil Disobedience, and its limits
sections.body_md:
- **Rich peasants** (Patidars of Gujarat, Jats of UP): hit by falling prices of commercial crops, they refused revenue and wanted it reduced; disappointed when the movement ended in 1931 without a revenue cut, many stayed away in 1932.
- **Poor peasants**: wanted unpaid **rent remitted**; many joined radical movements led by Socialists and Communists, since the Congress was unwilling to back no-rent campaigns that would upset rich peasants and landlords.
- **Business classes**: had prospered during the war; formed the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress (**1920**) and **FICCI (1927)**, with leaders such as **Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G.D. Birla**. They wanted protection against foreign goods and gave funds and refused imports. After the Round Table Conference failed they feared militant activity, prolonged disruption and socialism among young Congress members.
- **Industrial workers**: joined in large numbers only in the **Nagpur** region; railway (1930) and dock (1932) strikes; the Congress kept workers' demands out to avoid alienating industrialists.
- **Women**: took part on a large scale, mostly from high-caste urban and rich peasant families; the Congress was reluctant to give them positions of authority.

**Limits.** **Dalits**: Gandhiji called them *harijans* and campaigned against untouchability; **Dr B.R. Ambedkar** formed the **Depressed Classes Association (1930)** and demanded **separate electorates** at the Second Round Table Conference. When the British accepted, Gandhiji fasted unto death; the **Poona Pact (September 1932)** gave the Depressed Classes **reserved seats** in provincial and central councils, elected by the **general electorate**. **Muslims**: after non-cooperation many felt distant from a Congress seen as close to Hindu religious groups such as the **Hindu Mahasabha**; communal clashes followed. **Jinnah** offered to drop separate electorates for reserved seats in the Central Assembly and proportional representation in **Bengal and Punjab**, but at the **All Parties Conference (1928)** **M.R. Jayakar** of the Hindu Mahasabha opposed compromise.

key_terms.definition_md: A system in which only members of a community vote to elect that community's representatives.
Seats in a legislature set aside for a group, though all voters may vote for them.
The term used at the time for castes treated as untouchable; later called Scheduled Castes.

sections.heading: 6. The sense of collective belonging
sections.body_md:
- **Bharat Mata.** **Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay** wrote **"Vande Mataram"** in the 1870s as a hymn to the motherland; it later appeared in his novel ***Anandamath*** and was widely sung in the Swadeshi movement in Bengal. **Abanindranath Tagore** painted Bharat Mata as a calm, ascetic, spiritual figure; later images took many forms, and devotion to the mother figure came to be seen as proof of nationalism.
- **Folklore.** Nationalists believed folk tales, songs and legends held the true culture of the people. **Rabindranath Tagore** collected ballads, nursery rhymes and myths; **Natesa Sastri** published the four-volume ***The Folklore of Southern India***.
- **Flags and symbols.** The **Swadeshi flag** of Bengal: red, green and yellow, with **eight lotuses** for the provinces of British India and a **crescent moon** for Hindus and Muslims. By **1921** Gandhiji had designed the **Swaraj flag**: red, green and white with a **spinning wheel** in the centre. Carrying the flag in processions became an act of defiance.
- **History.** Nationalist writers retold India's achievements in **art, architecture, science, mathematics, religion, law and philosophy**, answering British claims that Indians were backward and urging pride.
- **Limits.** Images and histories drawn mainly from a **Hindu** past could make people of **other communities** feel left out.

key_terms.definition_md: The image of India as a mother figure, used to inspire devotion to the nation.
Traditional tales, songs, sayings and legends of ordinary people.
Using goods made in one's own country in place of foreign ones.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Swapping **Calcutta** (Sept 1920, leaders agree) and **Nagpur** (Dec 1920, programme adopted).
- Mixing up **Champaran** (indigo) and **Kheda** (revenue relief after crop failure and plague).
- Writing that the **Poona Pact** gave separate electorates: it gave **reserved seats** elected by the general electorate.
- Confusing **revenue** (paid by landowning peasants to the government) and **rent** (paid by tenants to landlords).
- Describing civil disobedience without saying what was new: people were asked to **break laws**.

**How marks are earned**
- Source-based (4 marks): (a) and (b) one precise fact each; (c) two points, one from the source and one from your knowledge, about 40 words.
- 3-mark answers: three distinct points, 40–60 words. 5-mark answers: five numbered points, about 120 words; "evaluate" needs a position, evidence and a counter-point.
- Map work: one mark per place, a dot and a clear label.
- On Gandhiji and Ambedkar, or Jinnah and the Congress, explain each side's reasons fairly.

cards.back_md: **War loans and higher taxes** (customs, new income tax), **prices doubled** 1913–18, and **forced recruitment** in villages.

cards.back_md: **Champaran 1917**: indigo peasants. **Kheda 1917–18**: peasants seeking revenue relief after crop failure and plague. **Ahmedabad 1918**: cotton mill workers.
Sweeping powers to repress political activity and detention **without trial for two years**.
**13 April 1919**, Amritsar, **General Dyer**; troops fired on a Baisakhi crowd in an enclosed ground.
The brothers **Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali**.

cards.back_md: To build **Hindu–Muslim unity** in a broad-based movement.
The British could rule only with **Indian help**; withdraw that help and their rule would fall.
**Calcutta (Sept)**: leaders persuaded to start non-cooperation. **Nagpur (Dec)**: compromise and programme **adopted**.

cards.back_md: **Khadi** cost more than mill cloth; **Indian institutions** came up slowly.

cards.front_md: Which province did not boycott the council elections, and why?
cards.back_md: **Madras**: the non-Brahman **Justice Party** saw the council as a route to power.
A sanyasi, once an **indentured labourer in Fiji**, who led the **Awadh** peasants against talukdars.
Forced labour **without payment**.
Social boycott: barbers and washermen refused to serve oppressive landlords.
Led a **guerrilla** movement in the **Gudem Hills** (Andhra Pradesh); believed force was needed; executed **1924**.

cards.back_md: The **Inland Emigration Act (1859)** confined them; to them swaraj meant **freedom to go home**.
Violence at **Chauri Chaura** (Gorakhpur), **February 1922**.
Formed by **C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru** within the Congress to contest council elections.

cards.back_md: It had **no Indian member** but was to decide India's constitutional future.

Used by **rich and poor**; taxed, with manufacture a **government monopoly**: a grievance that could unite all.

cards.back_md: Rich (Patidars, Jats): wanted **revenue** cut. Poor: wanted **rent** remitted; Congress avoided no-rent campaigns.
**FICCI (1927)**, Thakurdas, Birla: wanted protection from imports; drew back fearing **disruption and socialism**.

Give **one point from the source** and **one from your own knowledge**, about 40 words.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes **satyagraha** as Gandhiji practised it?

options.text_md: A non-violent struggle built on truth, which tries to win over the opponent's conscience instead of defeating him by force
An armed rising planned in secret against the colonial police
A campaign of petitions sent only through the legislative councils
A total ban on trade with every foreign country

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Satyagraha means insisting on truth. Gandhiji held that a person fighting for a just cause did not need force: by suffering patiently and without violence, the satyagrahi could appeal to the oppressor's conscience.
Step 2: So (a).
Step 3: (b) uses force, which satyagraha rejects; (c) is the moderate method of petitions, not mass action; (d) exaggerates: boycott of foreign goods was one tactic, not the meaning of satyagraha.

questions.stem_md: In 1917 Gandhiji went to Champaran in Bihar to support

options.text_md: cotton mill workers demanding better wages
peasants who could not pay land revenue after their crops failed
peasants struggling against the harsh indigo plantation system
tea-garden workers who wanted to return to their villages

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Champaran (north-west Bihar) was an indigo-growing district where planters forced peasants into an oppressive system of cultivation.
Step 2: So (c).
Step 3: (a) is the Ahmedabad mill workers' satyagraha (1918); (b) is Kheda in Gujarat; (d) refers to Assam plantation workers in 1921.

questions.stem_md: An imagined petition from a group of villagers in Gujarat around 1918 reads: "Our crops have failed, plague has visited our homes, and we cannot pay the land revenue this year. We ask only that collection be held back." Which early satyagraha of Gandhiji does this situation resemble most?

options.text_md: Ahmedabad
Kheda
Champaran
Dandi

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The clues are Gujarat, crop failure, plague and a request for relief from revenue.
Step 2: These match the peasants of **Kheda** district, whom Gandhiji supported in 1917–18, so (b).
Step 3: Ahmedabad (1918) was about mill workers; Champaran (1917) was about indigo planters in Bihar; Dandi (1930) was the end-point of the Salt March.

questions.stem_md: Why did Indians across the country protest against the Rowlatt Act of 1919?

options.text_md: It introduced a new tax on salt.
It shut Indians out of forests where they grazed cattle.
It doubled the land revenue paid by peasants.
It gave the government sweeping powers to crush political activity, including detention without trial for two years.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The Rowlatt Act was rushed through the Imperial Legislative Council although every Indian member opposed it.
Step 2: It allowed political prisoners to be held without trial for two years and armed the government against political activity, so (d).
Step 3: The salt tax was much older (and the target in 1930); forest closure and revenue were rural grievances, not the content of this Act.

questions.stem_md: Gandhiji's call for a nationwide satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act began with a hartal on

options.text_md: 6 April 1919
13 April 1919
26 January 1930
12 March 1930

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The protest opened with a hartal (closure of shops and work) on **6 April 1919**, so (a).
Step 2: 13 April 1919 is the date of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre; 26 January 1930 was the first Independence Day; 12 March 1930 was the start of the Salt March.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the events at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar on 13 April 1919 is correct?

options.text_md: The crowd had gathered for a session of the Indian National Congress.
General Dyer closed the exits and ordered his troops to fire on the crowd, many of whom had come for the Baisakhi fair and did not know martial law had been imposed.
Gandhiji was arrested at the meeting and the crowd attacked the police.
The firing led Gandhiji to withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: On Baisakhi day a large crowd, including villagers who had come for the fair and were unaware of martial law, gathered in the enclosed ground. General Dyer blocked the exits and opened fire, killing hundreds.
Step 2: So (b).
Step 3: (a) is false: it was not a Congress session. (c) is false: Gandhiji was not there. (d) confuses it with Chauri Chaura (1922); the Non-Cooperation Movement had not yet begun.

questions.stem_md: The Khilafat Committee, formed in Bombay in March 1919, was led by

options.text_md: Chitta Ranjan Das and Motilal Nehru
Muhammad Ali Jinnah and M.R. Jayakar
the brothers Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali
Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan and Jawaharlal Nehru

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The Khilafat Committee was formed to defend the Khalifa's temporal powers after the Ottoman defeat; the Ali brothers led it.
Step 2: So (c).
Step 3: Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party (1923); Jinnah and Jayakar appear in the 1928 negotiations; Ghaffar Khan led the movement in the North-West Frontier.

questions.stem_md: In his book *Hind Swaraj* (1909), Gandhiji argued that British rule had lasted in India because

options.text_md: Indians had cooperated with it, and if they stopped cooperating it would collapse
the British army was too strong to be defeated
Indians had never demanded self-government
the princely states protected it

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Gandhiji's argument was that the British ruled with Indian cooperation; withdraw that cooperation and the rule would fall within a year, and swaraj would come.
Step 2: This is the idea behind non-cooperation, so (a). The other options are not his argument.

questions.stem_md:
Consider two statements.

**I.** At the Calcutta session of September 1920, Gandhiji persuaded other leaders that a non-cooperation movement should be started in support of Khilafat as well as for swaraj.

**II.** At the Nagpur session of December 1920, a compromise was reached and the Non-Cooperation programme was adopted.

Which of these is/are correct?

options.text_md: Only I
Only II
Both I and II
Neither I nor II

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Statement I is correct: in Calcutta (September 1920) Gandhiji won over other leaders to the plan.
Step 2: Statement II is correct: many in Congress were still unsure, and at Nagpur (December 1920) a compromise was worked out and the programme adopted.
Step 3: So (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following was **not** part of the programme of the Non-Cooperation Movement as planned in 1920?

options.text_md: Giving up titles awarded by the government
Boycotting government schools, courts and legislative councils
Boycotting foreign goods
Making salt from sea water in defiance of the law

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Non-cooperation began with surrender of titles and went on to boycott civil services, the army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods.
Step 2: Breaking the salt law belongs to the **Civil Disobedience Movement** of 1930, so (d).

questions.stem_md: During the Non-Cooperation Movement, council elections were boycotted in most provinces. In which province did a party of non-Brahmans contest them because it saw the council as a way to gain power?

options.text_md: Bengal
Madras
Punjab
United Provinces

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In Madras, the **Justice Party**, a party of non-Brahmans, felt that entering the council gave it a way to win a share of power that had usually gone to Brahmans.
Step 2: So (b).

questions.stem_md: Imagine a college student in Lahore who left his government college in 1921 to join the movement and returned to it in 1922. Which reason, true of the movement in the cities, best explains his return?

options.text_md: The government had abolished college fees.
Gandhiji had ordered all students to go back in 1921.
Indian-run national schools and colleges had come up too slowly to take in all the students who had left.
Khadi had become cheaper than mill cloth.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In the towns, non-cooperation lost force partly because the alternative Indian institutions needed time to be set up; students and teachers began going back to government schools, and lawyers to the courts.
Step 2: So (c).
Step 3: (a) is invented; (b) is wrong, the call was to leave, not return; (d) is the opposite of the truth: khadi was usually dearer, which was another reason for the slowdown.

questions.stem_md: The peasant movement in Awadh against talukdars and landlords was led by Baba Ramchandra, who was

options.text_md: a lawyer from Bombay
a sanyasi who had earlier gone to Fiji as an indentured labourer
a leader of the Justice Party
a mill owner from Ahmedabad

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Baba Ramchandra was a sanyasi who had worked in Fiji as an indentured labourer before returning to lead the peasants of Awadh.
Step 2: So (b).

questions.stem_md: In an imagined Awadh village in 1920, the barber and the washerman stop serving the family of a landlord who has evicted tenants. This form of protest was called

options.text_md: a hartal
picketing
a nai-dhobi bandh
begar

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Peasant panchayats in Awadh organised social boycotts in which landlords were denied the services of barbers (nai) and washermen (dhobi).
Step 2: This is a **nai-dhobi bandh**, so (c).
Step 3: A hartal is a closure of shops and work; picketing is standing outside a shop to stop people entering; **begar** is forced unpaid labour, the very thing peasants protested against.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about Alluri Sitarama Raju is correct?

options.text_md: He led a guerrilla struggle in the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh and, unlike Gandhiji, believed force was necessary to win freedom.
He led the tea-garden workers of Assam out of the plantations.
He founded the Swaraj Party with C.R. Das.
He was a mill owner who financed the Civil Disobedience Movement.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In the early 1920s Raju led the tribal people of the Gudem Hills in a guerrilla movement. He spoke of Gandhiji with respect and was inspired by non-cooperation, yet held that India could be freed only by force. His followers attacked police stations; he was captured and executed in 1924.
Step 2: So (a). The other options belong to different groups or people.

questions.stem_md: Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859, tea-garden workers in Assam could not leave the plantations without permission. When thousands walked out in 1921, what did "swaraj" most likely mean to them?

options.text_md: Being free to come and go from the plantations and to return to the villages they had come from
A reduction in the salt tax
Winning seats in the provincial legislative councils
Separate electorates for plantation workers

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The workers were confined to the gardens by law. Hearing of non-cooperation, many left and set out for home.
Step 2: For them swaraj meant freedom of movement and a return to their villages, so (a).
Step 3: Council seats were an elite concern; the salt tax became the issue only in 1930; separate electorates were not their demand.

questions.stem_md: Gandhiji called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922 after

options.text_md: the Simon Commission arrived in India
a clash between a crowd and the police at Chauri Chaura turned violent
the Gandhi–Irwin Pact was signed
the Rowlatt Act was withdrawn

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: At Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur district, United Provinces), a peaceful demonstration in a bazaar ended in a violent clash with the police.
Step 2: Gandhiji judged that people were not yet disciplined enough for non-violent mass action, so he withdrew the movement: (b).
Step 3: The Simon Commission came in 1928 and the Gandhi–Irwin Pact was signed in 1931.

questions.stem_md: C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress because they wanted to

options.text_md: restart the Khilafat agitation
organise tribal peasants for armed struggle
boycott all elections permanently
contest elections to the provincial councils and oppose British policies from inside them

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: After 1922 some leaders were weary of mass struggle and wanted to take part in elections to the councils set up by the Government of India Act of 1919.
Step 2: They argued that members could expose and oppose government policies from within the councils, so (d).

questions.stem_md: Why did nationalists greet the Simon Commission with the slogan "Go back Simon" when it arrived in 1928?

options.text_md: It had no Indian member, although it was to report on India's constitutional future.
It had been appointed by the Congress without consulting the Muslim League.
It proposed to abolish the provincial councils.
It was led by the Viceroy, Lord Irwin.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The Commission was set up by the Tory government in Britain to examine India's constitutional system and suggest changes, but all its members were British.
Step 2: Being left out of decisions about their own future angered Indians, so (a).
Step 3: It was not appointed by the Congress, made no such proposal at arrival, and was headed by Sir John Simon, not the Viceroy.

questions.stem_md: The Lahore session of the Congress in December 1929 is remembered because it

options.text_md: adopted the Non-Cooperation programme
accepted the offer of dominion status
formalised the demand for **Purna Swaraj** under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru
decided to join the First Round Table Conference

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Under Jawaharlal Nehru's presidency the Lahore Congress made complete independence (Purna Swaraj) its goal, and 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day.
Step 2: So (c).
Step 3: Non-cooperation was adopted at Nagpur (1920); Irwin's vague offer of dominion status did not satisfy the Congress; the Congress stayed away from the First Round Table Conference.

questions.stem_md: Why did Gandhiji choose the salt tax as the issue on which to launch the Civil Disobedience Movement?

options.text_md: Only rich merchants used salt, so they would fund the movement.
Salt was eaten by rich and poor alike, so a tax on it was a grievance that could unite everyone, and the government's monopoly over making it was easy to defy.
The Congress had already won the right to make salt at the Lahore session.
Breaking the salt law carried no punishment.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Salt was an everyday necessity for every household. Taxing it, and keeping its production a government monopoly, made British rule appear oppressive to all.
Step 2: Anyone living near the coast could defy the law by making salt, so (b).
Step 3: (a), (c) and (d) are false: salt was not a luxury, the Lahore session won no such right, and salt-makers were arrested.

questions.stem_md: What was the main difference between the Civil Disobedience Movement and the Non-Cooperation Movement?

options.text_md: Civil Disobedience was confined to towns, while Non-Cooperation spread to villages.
Non-Cooperation demanded Purna Swaraj, while Civil Disobedience asked only for dominion status.
Civil Disobedience allowed the use of force against the police.
Civil Disobedience called on people to break colonial laws openly, going beyond refusing cooperation.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Non-cooperation meant withdrawing from British institutions. Civil disobedience went a step further: people were to **break** colonial laws, such as the salt law and the forest laws.
Step 2: So (d).
Step 3: Both movements spread to villages; both were meant to be non-violent; and it was Civil Disobedience that came after the Purna Swaraj resolution.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Patidar farmer in Gujarat joined the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930 by refusing to pay revenue, but stayed away when the movement was restarted in 1932. Which explanation fits the history of rich peasants best?

options.text_md: The government had already halved revenue rates in 1931.
He had become a supporter of separate electorates.
Congress had begun a no-rent campaign against him as a landlord.
The movement had been called off in 1931 without revenue rates being revised, and he felt let down.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Rich peasant communities such as the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh joined because the trade depression and falling prices made their cash-crop incomes collapse while the revenue demand stayed high.
Step 2: When the movement was called off in 1931 without any change in revenue rates, many were deeply disappointed and refused to join in 1932, so (d).
Step 3: (a) is false; (b) is unrelated; (c) is the opposite: the Congress was unwilling to back no-rent campaigns in most places.

questions.stem_md: After the failure of the Round Table Conference, Indian business groups were no longer uniformly enthusiastic about Civil Disobedience. Which of the following was **not** a reason for this?

options.text_md: They were worried about the spread of militant activities.
They feared that business would be disrupted for a long time.
They were uneasy about the growing influence of socialism among younger Congress members.
The government had agreed to remove all duties on imported cloth.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Industrialists were alarmed by militant activity, by the prospect of prolonged disruption and by socialist ideas among young Congress members.
Step 2: Removing duties on imported cloth would have hurt Indian industry and was not something the government had agreed to; it is not a reason. So (d).

questions.stem_md: Under the Poona Pact of September 1932, the Depressed Classes (later called the Scheduled Castes)

options.text_md: received reserved seats in the provincial and central legislative councils, to be filled through voting by the general electorate
received separate electorates in which only they could vote for their candidates
were given no seats at all
were placed under the Muslim League for representation

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Ambedkar had won separate electorates from the British. Gandhiji, believing this would divide Hindu society and slow the integration of Dalits, fasted unto death.
Step 2: The compromise, the Poona Pact, gave the Depressed Classes **reserved seats** in the councils, but voters of the **general electorate** would elect them: (a).

questions.stem_md: Hopes of resolving the question of Muslim representation faded at the All Parties Conference of 1928 when

options.text_md: Gandhiji refused to attend
M.R. Jayakar of the Hindu Mahasabha strongly opposed efforts at compromise
the British government banned the conference
Muhammad Ali Jinnah demanded a separate country

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Jinnah had been willing to give up the demand for separate electorates if Muslims were assured reserved seats in the Central Assembly and representation in proportion to population in Muslim-majority provinces (Bengal and Punjab).
Step 2: At the 1928 conference M.R. Jayakar of the Hindu Mahasabha strongly opposed a compromise, so (b).
Step 3: (d) is wrong for 1928: no such demand was made at that conference.

questions.stem_md: An imagined museum label describes a flag: "Three bands of red, green and white, with a spinning wheel at the centre, designed by 1921." Which flag is this?

options.text_md: The Swadeshi flag of Bengal, with eight lotuses and a crescent moon
The British Union Jack
The Swaraj flag designed by Gandhiji
The flag of the Khilafat Committee

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: By 1921 Gandhiji had designed the **Swaraj flag**: a tricolour of red, green and white with a spinning wheel in the centre, standing for the Gandhian ideal of self-help.
Step 2: So (c).
Step 3: The Swadeshi flag (red, green and yellow) had eight lotuses for the eight provinces of British India and a crescent moon for Hindus and Muslims.

questions.stem_md: Who painted a famous early image of Bharat Mata as a calm, ascetic figure, and who wrote the hymn "Vande Mataram"?

options.text_md: Abanindranath Tagore; Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
Rabindranath Tagore; Natesa Sastri
Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay; Abanindranath Tagore
Raja Ravi Varma; Rabindranath Tagore

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote "Vande Mataram" in the 1870s as a hymn to the motherland; it later appeared in his novel *Anandamath*.
Step 2: Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata as an ascetic, calm and spiritual figure. So (a).
Step 3: Rabindranath Tagore collected folk material; Natesa Sastri published Tamil folk tales; (c) reverses the pair.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following was **not** a result of the First World War in India?

options.text_md: Defence spending rose sharply, paid for by war loans and higher taxes.
Prices roughly doubled between 1913 and 1918.
Villages were pressed to supply soldiers through forced recruitment.
Income tax was abolished to win popular support.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The war raised defence expenditure; customs duties went up and **income tax was introduced**, not abolished.
Step 2: Prices doubled between 1913 and 1918, and forced recruitment caused anger in rural areas.
Step 3: So the statement that is not a result is (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** All the Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council opposed the Rowlatt Act.

**Reason (R):** The Act allowed the government to keep political prisoners in detention without trial for two years.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: the Act was passed in spite of the united opposition of the Indian members.
Step 2: R is true, and it is the reason for their opposition: the Act took away basic legal protections. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The boycott of foreign cloth lost force in the towns after some time.

**Reason (R):** Khadi was often more expensive than mill-made cloth, so poorer people could not afford to buy it for long.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: the economic boycott could not be kept up for long in the cities.
Step 2: R is true, and it explains A: hand-spun, hand-woven cloth cost more than mass-produced cloth, which poorer buyers could not afford. So (a). (Slow growth of alternative institutions was another reason.)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In 1921 houses of talukdars and merchants in parts of Awadh were attacked and grain hoards were taken over.

**Reason (R):** Gandhiji had told the peasants that land would be redistributed and no taxes need be paid.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: as the movement spread in 1921, some peasant action in Awadh turned violent.
Step 2: R is false: Gandhiji had given no such instruction. Local leaders used his name to justify actions he and the Congress did not approve of.
Step 3: So (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The rebels of the Gudem Hills attacked police stations and tried to kill British officials.

**Reason (R):** People believed that Alluri Sitarama Raju had special powers, such as making accurate astrological predictions and healing the sick.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: the rebels carried on guerrilla warfare for swaraj.
Step 2: R is true: Raju was believed to have such powers.
Step 3: But the attacks are explained by the tribal grievances (closure of forests, begar for road building) and Raju's belief that force was needed, not by his reputed powers. So (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Simon Commission was greeted with black flags and the slogan "Go back Simon" when it arrived in India in 1928.

**Reason (R):** The Commission was set up by the Tory government in Britain.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true: it was constituted by the Conservative (Tory) government.
Step 3: The protests were caused by the absence of any Indian member on a body deciding India's constitutional future, not by which British party appointed it. So (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Gandhiji began a fast unto death in 1932.

**Reason (R):** The British government had accepted Ambedkar's demand for separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true, and it is the reason: Gandhiji believed separate electorates would slow down the integration of the Depressed Classes into society, and fasted against them until the Poona Pact was agreed. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Industrial workers took part in the Civil Disobedience Movement in large numbers all over India.

**Reason (R):** The Congress was reluctant to include workers' demands in its programme, fearing it would alienate industrialists.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is false: except in the Nagpur region, industrial workers did not join in large numbers.
Step 2: R is true: the Congress held back from workers' demands so as not to drive away industrialists and divide the anti-imperial forces.
Step 3: So (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Gandhiji and his volunteers walked about 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi over 24 days.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The Salt March began on 12 March 1930 with 78 volunteers and reached Dandi on 6 April, covering about 240 miles in 24 days (around 10 miles a day).
Step 2: True.

questions.stem_md: True or false? During the Civil Disobedience Movement the Congress readily gave women positions of authority within the organisation.

options.text_md: True
